entry.title: Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross Are Back at It (Scoring David Fincher Movies)
entry.summary: The duo’s work on The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth will be their sixth collaboration
entry.content:
Like David Fincher was going to get someone else to score The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Pitchfork can confirm the filmmaker has reunited with longtime collaborators Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross for his forthcoming Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood spinoff. It hits theaters November 25, with a Netflix premiere set for December 23. The film stars Brad Pitt, reprising his role as Booth, alongside Elizabeth Debicki, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, and Scott Caan.

The Nine Inch Nails duo have scored Fincher’s last six movies, dating back to 2010’s The Social Network, which netted them Oscars for Best Original Score. You can revisit some of their film work in our rundown of The 50 Best Movie Scores of All Time.

entry.title: Yaeji Plots a Dance Dance Revolution in New Single “DDR”
entry.summary: The singer-producer’s first song of the year is a collaboration with Enayet and K Wata
entry.content:
Yaeji has stepped back up to the plate with a Dance Dance Revolution-themed song—her latest in a string of standalone singles following 2023’s With a Hammer. Out on XL and created alongside Enayet and K Wata, “DDR” comes with a footwork-heavy video directed by Giseong Jun. Watch it below.

Yaeji elaborated on the idea behind the track in the YouTube caption: “i had this thought while out one night in nyc: if our current world is suffocating us then what does the reality we wanna see actually look like? maybe we’re actually experiencing a dance dance ‘revolution.’ the miracle of all our bodies on the dancefloor in the same place at the same time. we’re making sure there’s water and choosing to protect each other so no one’s getting harassed, all while on our own introspective journeys soundtracked by the music. this one is for you. it’s also for me.”

To celebrate the single, Yaeji is hosting an all-night DDR party at Paragon in Brooklyn this Friday, November 6, sharing the bill with DJ Swisha, OSSX, Lil C, and DJ Noir. “DDR,” Yaeji’s first single of 2026, follows last year’s “Pondeggi” and the Underscores and Aliyah’s Interlude collaboration “Booboo2.”

entry.title: Listen to Sufjan Stevens’ New Song “On This Christmas (It Only Gets Better)”
entry.summary: He dug into the vault for his holiday compilation Worst Christmas Ever!
entry.content:
Halloween may be barely behind us but Sufjan Stevens is already in the holiday spirit. His forthcoming compilation Worst Christmas Ever! compiles a mix of Yuletide standards done up Stevens style (“Angels We Have Heard on High (Christmas Infinity Voyage Version)”) and originals from his extensive holiday catalog. Among them is a new track, “On This Christmas (It Only Gets Better),” which you can now listen to below. Worst Christmas Ever! is out November 6 via Asthmatic Kitty.

Stevens’ love for Christmas is well-documented; according to a statement, he has written and recorded more than 100 Christmas songs since 2001. Worst Christmas Ever! features a number of tracks that previously appeared on his Songs for Christmas, Vols. 1-5 and the 2012 box set Silver & Gold: Songs for Christmas, Vols. 6-10. Collaborators across the record include the National’s Aaron and Bryce Dessner, Arcade Fire’s Richard Reed Parry, Cat Martino, Gabriel Kahane, and Casey Foubert.

Although Stevens hasn’t debuted a new album since 2023’s Javelin, he has remained active on the release front. In 2024, he shared a 20th anniversary reissue of Seven Swans. Last year, he celebrated a decade of Carrie & Lowell with its own reissue, and released the song “Heaven Thunder” with Mina Tindle. In September, Stevens made a surprise appearance at Meg Lui’s show in Kingston, New York, marking his first public musical performance in over eight years, following a 2023 diagnosis with Guillain-Barré syndrome, a rare disorder in which the body’s immune system attacks the nerves.

entry.title: Juan Atkins, Co-Founder of Techno Music, Dies at 64
entry.summary: The Detroit producer and DJ pioneered the genre as a solo artist and member of the Belleville Three, Cybotron, and Borderland
entry.content:
Juan Atkins, the lifelong producer and DJ who co-founded Detroit techno music, has died; Green Smith Artists, Atkins’ management company, confirmed his death. Atkins was slated to perform at Yu Yu Club in Mexico City last night (October 31). He was 64.

As a member of the Belleville Three, Cybotron, and Borderland, Atkins’ impact on electronic music is, at this point, incalculable. By age 18, he had formed Cybotron with his friend Richard “3070” Davis. By merging funk, electronic instrumentation, and futuristic themes, they helped redirect the genre’s sound with their early singles—“Alleys of the Mind,” “Cosmic Raindance,” “Cosmic Cars,” “The Line”—before fully dominating the dancefloor with “Clear” in 1983. The electro track became an instant underground hit and soon broke into the mainstream. The single sold 50,000 copies and became a genre-defining composition, famously sampled by Missy Elliott and countless others. The duo went on to release three albums: 1983’s Enter, 1993’s Empathy, and 1995’s Cyber Ghetto.

As a born-and-raised Detroiter, Atkins was part of the community’s local music scene at an early age, playing in funk and garage bands with his friends and being raised by a father who worked as a concert promoter. After meeting Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson in junior high school, Atkins shifted his focus from guitar and bass to digitized instruments, purchasing his first-ever synthesizer, a Korg MS-10, when he turned 15. The friends later earned the nickname the Belleville Three due to their close-knit status as collaborative musicians shaping their electronic scene and sharing equipment, studio space, and production work.

For Atkins, there was more to it than just making people get lost in the trance of dancing. “My lyrics are supposed to make you think about something other than shaking your booty on the dancefloor and falling in love,” he recently told The Guardian. “I feel like artists have an obligation to say something meaningful.”

In 2005, Atkins told Pitchfork that he “always called the music [he] was making techno music” despite DJs in the neighboring Chicago scene, like Derrick Carter and Frankie Knuckles, labeling it Detroit house music. “When you listen to Chicago records, a lot of them sounded like Philly International records,” said Atkins. “They were always like the Philly International disco sound. Going ‘ks-ks-ks-ks…’ you know! That’s the whole difference. In Detroit, we don’t have any real reference point. All the Detroit stuff was pure futuristic. The only thing that we really had in common was the form… There was definitely competition between the Chicago and the Detroit DJs. We all wanted to be famous. But we were also friends, Tyree Cooper and all of these guys. Farley was a good friend. We went to Farley in Chicago just to hang out and they came to Detroit.”

Atkins stayed active as a touring DJ and performer on through to the end. In his final two years, Atkins could be seen everywhere from New York City to Berlin playing in clubs, or on the main stage at festivals like Detroit’s Movement Festival, Amsterdam’s Dekmantel Festival, and England’s Houghton Festival.

This is a developing story.

entry.title: Listen to the First Atlas Sound Song in 15 Years
entry.summary: “Octoberland” also arrives with a music video
entry.content:
Bradford Cox’s return to the stage was already cause for celebration. When Atlas Sound, his long-dormant solo project, was added to the bill of Philadelphia’s Making Time ∞ festival last month, the Deerhunter frontman hadn’t performed live since 2019, save an impromptu noise set at an Athens, GA vintage market in 2023. What few could have predicted was that Cox would debut a whole album’s worth of all-new material. His eight-song set, which I was blessed to experience firsthand, was sparsely arranged—the accompaniment amounted to a set of brass bells, a bass guitar, and Cox’s trusty SP-404—yet transfixing all the same.

Now, you can hear one of those songs in its full-fledged studio incarnation. It’s called “Octoberland” and it also arrives with a haunting music video, directed by Cox himself. Check it out below.

The name Atlas Sound originates from a cassette karaoke machine that a middle-school-age Cox used to create his earliest recordings. Between 2008 and 2011, he put out three albums under the moniker—Let the Blind Lead Those Who Can See But Cannot Feel, Logos, and Parallax—plus the demo collection Bedroom Databank, Vols. 1-4. These records deviated from Deerhunter’s shoegaze and krautrock leanings, placing a greater emphasis on sampling and wall-of-sound pop.

For anyone who missed Atlas Sound at Making Time, fret not: Cox has three more festival dates planned in 2027: Big Ears in Knoxville, Kilby Block Party in Salt Lake City, and Primavera Sound in Barcelona.

Read about Logos at No. 20 in The 30 Best Dream Pop Albums.

entry.title: Lily Allen Dressed as an Empty Ticketmaster Map for Halloween
entry.summary: After scaling down her summer tour, Allen dressed up as every pop star’s nightmare: a pox of unsold tickets
entry.content:
Lily Allen, shameless pop ironist and self-satirist, has never shied from public vitriol—a quality that has come in handy as fans have reacted to her live shows behind West End Girl. Some lamented the format—essentially a full-length rendition of the LP, nothing more; venues were downsized as excitement (and prurient interest in the album’s salacious subject matter) began to dull. But like any good pop trickster, Allen has turned a potential PR crisis into an opportunity for mischief: in this case, blue-dot fever (the term du jour for a Ticketmaster seat plan full of unsold tickets) made manifest in a spotty blue onesie and jacket.

The initial UK tour behind the album, dubbed Lily Allen Performs West End Girl, was intended for smaller venues and theaters, hinting that fans should expect few bells and whistles. But early demand enticed her to scale up: theaters turned into arenas, and dates around the world, including in the United States, ballooned the itinerary.

When the run got under way, however, Allen was forced to address criticism of the format. “It’s my artistic choice not to talk to the audience, the fourth wall helps with the storytelling,” she wrote on X. “Most people find it to be effective.” She added, “I don’t want anyone to feel ripped off, Everyone on this tour is really working very hard to give people the best show we possibly can, and I’m extremely proud of it.”

Two weeks later, Allen downscaled the North American itinerary, swapping several big arenas for small arenas and small arenas for amphitheaters. A planned Montreal date got the ax, though a Seattle show was added. Now, she is ready to smile about it. “Never beating the allegations,” she wrote on Instagram. “#bluedotfever.”

entry.title: 8 New Albums You Should Listen to Now: Diiv, Queens of the Stone Age, and More
entry.summary: Stream new releases from Diiv, Queens of the Stone Age, Kali Malone, and more
entry.content:
With so much good music being released all the time, it can be hard to determine what to listen to first. Every week, Pitchfork offers a run-down of significant new releases available on streaming services. This week’s batch includes new albums from DIIV, Kali Malone, Queens of the Stone Age, and more. Subscribe to Pitchfork’s New Music Friday newsletter to get our recommendations in your inbox every week. (All releases featured here are independently selected by our editors. When you buy something through our affiliate links, however, Pitchfork earns an affiliate commission.)

Diiv: ZIRP! [Fantasy]

Despite writing the new Diiv album in a period of chaos—welcoming his second child amid fallout from the destruction of his home in the Altadena wildfires—Zachary Cole Smith went into ZIRP! in a spirit of unbridled, determined fun. Buoyed along by an unlikely producer in A. G. Cook, the band compacts its trademark shoegaze sound into nuggets of electro-pop joy, the smothering haze coexisting with effervescent hooks that go down as easily as pop-punk alcopops.

Andy Stott: Late Loop [Modern Love]

For Andy Stott’s music to hit hardest, close your eyes, take a deep breath, and envision the world in slow motion. The electronic producer moves carefully through every song, as if reducing listeners’ heartbeats is the trick to making them see everything around them. On his first album in five years, Late Loop, Stott transformed experimental drone into downtempo trance songs by enlisting vocalists Alison Skidmore and Elaine Howley to articulate a few observations—how pressure leads to escape, or mirrors can extend forever—that turn into mantras.

Heathers: Awesome [Warner]

Do you miss when rock bands were mostly teenagers pissing off their parents by practicing too loud in the basement? If the answer is yes, you’re primed to love the debut album of 23-year-old Heath Michael Thomas, who performs under the name Heathers. Thomas has been making music since he was 11, and recorded the bulk of his 14-track debut at home in Missouri. Driving and dextrous garage rock riffs get their hooks in quick and deep, and that’s before Thomas even graces the mic, whether he’s screaming, snarling, or whispering. He channels the distinct euphoria-meets-malaise of school being out for summer.

Brat Star: Southern Ontario Gothic [Pre Lapsarian]

Head-to-toe Aritzia. Kill Bill murder techniques. Dirty Hokas. The notorious crack-smoking Toronto mayor Rob Ford. All these influences and more converge on the Toronto-based artist and reformed Berlin DJ Brat Star’s debut album Southern Ontario Gothic, which pairs the deadpan chatter-sing of Sidney Gish and Frankie Cosmos with muted Drain Gang swagger and 2010s pop radio production primarily handled herself, with some assists from close collaborator Loukeman.

Dream Unending: Certain Uncertainties [20 Buck Spin]

Dream Unending, the duo of Tomb Mold’s Derrick Vella and Innumerable Forms’ Justin DeTore, do doom metal a little differently. Their third album, Certain Uncertainties, often spends minutes sounding like a lost '70s prog record, old Western soundtrack, or roots rock demo EP before Detore’s rumbling vocals and death-drop drum lines descend onto Vella’s extended guitar solos like a Balrog. Although they get assists from trumpeter Leila Abdul-Rauf, percussionist Benny Grotto, and vocalist Brendan Radigan, they primarily go toe-to-toe, underscoring their delightfully odd-couple pairing.

Lydia Loveless: Accolades [Bloodshot]

Last year, Lydia Loveless began releasing a song a month on Bandcamp, challenging themselves to stick to a steady routine and stay creative at the same time. This attention to craft resulted in a number of songs featured on their new EP Accolades, a collection of alt-country and classic rock tunes backed by a sturdy enough band—get a load of that Farfisa organ on “What We Learned”—to let Loveless really flex as a songwriter. There‘s a touch of Billy Joel to “Avoiding Highways,” and some Tom Petty optimism on the title track “Accolades,” resplendent with little lyrical gems like “I guess I'm just looking for a way to be as bored as the good old days.”

Queens of the Stone Age: Perfecth [Matador]

In the world of Queens of Stone Age, nobody’s perfect, but you can be perfecth. For a band that’s been around for three decades—and spent much of their 2023 album, In Times New Roman…, discussing how twisted, messy, and dark life can get—coming to terms with the inevitability of your own blemishes seems like the logical next step. On Perfecth, you can hear the band loosening their shoulders after a long, grueling battle with acceptance. In some of the stoner-rocker’s most relaxed and spacious music in years, they muse on heartbreak, sex, and purifying catharsis.

Kali Malone: Burning Song [Ideologic Organ]

J.S. Bach spent the last 27 years of his life working as the music director at Thomaskirche, a Lutheran church located in Leipzig, Germany. It’s the same location Kali Malone recorded music on two late nights in August with cellist Lucy Railton and Stephen O’Malley, who joined on bowed acoustic guitar. The session has now become Burning Song, a ruminative album that reveals its quiet beauty layer by layer, like ocean water slowly breaking down rock.

entry.title: Phoebe Bridgers and Billie Eilish Lend Their Voices to My Chemical Romance’s New Short Film
entry.summary: The band made the animated “Prelude to the End” with visual artist Lauren Tsai
entry.content:
My Chemical Romance have released a new animated short film with a pretty formidable voice cast, including Phoebe Bridgers, Billie Eilish, Hideo Kojima, and actor John C. McGinley. “Prelude to the End,” a collaboration with visual artist Lauren Tsai that incorporates The Black Parade track “The End,” arrives just after the band dropped a 20th anniversary reissue of the album. Check it out below.

“Prelude to the End” follows Astrid, a girl studying at a boarding school in New England overrun with trash. After falling down the school’s garbage chute in search of a beloved sketchbook, she enters a new, uncanny realm of old ideas that come to life. Bridgers voices Astrid’s sister, while Eilish lends her vocals to Astrid’s close friend. Kojima plays a character called the Teacher, and McGinley voices an even more imposing administrative figure, the Dean. The film includes a live recording of Pascal Dusapin’s Flying River, Violin Concerto, performed by Utopia Orchestra and conducted by Giuseppe Mengoli.

My Chemical Romance plan to screen the film at two forthcoming Hollywood Bowl shows on October 30 and 31. They mark the final two nights of the band’s five-night residency at the Los Angeles venue, part of a larger ongoing tour celebrating The Black Parade’s big 20th. The run kicked off last year, and MCR also played the record in full at the festival When We Were Young in 2024.

entry.title: Nick Valensi Is Busy Playing With Everyone But the Strokes
entry.summary: He’s on a “temporary break” from his longtime band—but not from performing with other artists
entry.content:
Rumors abound as to why Strokes guitarist Nick Valensi has been on indefinite hiatus from his longtime band since May, but that hasn’t stopped him from playing with other artists. Valensi’s spent the last few months shredding on stage with Jack White, Nigel Godrich and Dhani Harrison’s group Dragonflies, and, last night in Paris, Duran Duran.

“You might recognize him from the Strokes but tonight he’s here with us, the amazing guitarist, Nick Valensi,” said Simon Le Bon ahead of their performance of “Rio,” which they had to restart due to technical difficulties. “I don’t know how to fix shit like this,” Valensi said about the snafu. Julian Casablancas might be thinking the same.

entry.title: Junior Boys Return With New Album The Gore
entry.summary: “Underneath the Moon” leads the Canadian duo’s follow-up to Waiting Game
entry.content:
Jeremy Greenspan and Matt Didemus are back as Junior Boys for a new album, The Gore, which merges themes of grief and nostalgia with the influence of horror cinema. Out February 12 via City Slang, the album is led by the lysergic techno single “Underneath the Moon” and a video, directed by the artist John Smith, that will delight fans of TV static. Check it out below.

Greenspan said in a press release, “This song is deeply inspired by the 2022 horror film Skinamarink. I used old tape loop techniques using an old Tascam tape machine to achieve a number of the effects in the film, to work as a sort of homage to the ephemeral quality of analog recording tech.” He added that The Gore—written over several years, in the wake of the deaths of his father and a close friend—is a sort of twin to its predecessor, Waiting Game: “a polarized articulation of the same thing, something about Silence, Serenity, Terror and Time, both circular and unending.”

While there are no tour dates on the docket just yet, Junior Boys have lined up album playbacks early next year in Brooklyn, Seattle, and Toronto. Those will begin with screenings of the experimental film Wavelength and end with a Q&A with Greenspan.

entry.title: Maryland Is Getting Its Own (Mini) Sphere
entry.summary: The Prince George’s County Council has authorized up to $215 million for a venue just south of Washington, D.C.
entry.content:
East Coast concert lovers with a penchant for geodesic domes, rejoice: the Las Vegas Sphere is getting a sister venue in Maryland. WTOP reports that the Prince George’s County Council (PGCC) has approved up to $215 million in funding to build a Sphere on the Potomac River, just south of Washington, D.C.

The shape of the proposed Sphere at National Harbor will be the same, but the size will be smaller: where the Las Vegas Sphere can hold up to 20,000 people, the planned capacity for the Maryland venue is around 6,000. The new Sphere will be part of a larger complex. The PGCC voted unanimously on October 27 to push the project, which was first announced back in January, forward. Dates for both a groundbreaking ceremony and an opening have yet to be confirmed. All told, the venue is projected to cost around $1.4 billion.

“This project represents a $1.3 billion dollar economic impact to Prince George’s County and a $1.5 billion dollar impact to the state of Maryland,” County Executive Aisha Braveboy said in a news conference. “This project is projected to generate $63 million annually in just property tax and sales and amusement tax alone.” Earlier this month, the PGCC also approved a labor peace agreement that will allow Sphere workers to organize once it opens; however, this deal did not include the construction workers who will build the venue.

Since it opened in 2023, the Las Vegas Sphere has hosted large-scale residencies from U2, No Doubt, Dead & Company, Metallica, and more. Backstreet Boys, the Eagles, Carín Leon, and John Mayer all have upcoming shows slated at the venue.

entry.title: Watch Robyn Cover Tinashe’s “Popstar”

Robyn opened the performance with the first verse of “Punkrocker,” giving its iconic hook a new treatment by replacing “punkrocker” with “pop star,” before transitioning into the title track of Tinashe’s recent pop manifesto.

entry.title: Xaviersobased Wants to Collab With Sabrina Carpenter
entry.summary: “Bro, I’ll knock out a whole album with her”
entry.content:
Xaviersobased has worked with OsamaSon, Lil B, and Skrillex but he has his sights set a bit higher on the Hot 100.

In a new Hypebeast cover story, the New York rapper was asked whether he would consider chart-chasing with a feature from a pop star like Sabrina Carpenter. “Bro, I’ll knock out a whole album with her,” he said. “I’m down for all types of things, but it just has to feel right and be done in a certain way.”

It’s difficult to imagine what a Xav/Sab joint would sound like—Carpenter singing something desperately horny over blown-out beats? Xaviersobased rapping over disco-pop?—but we’re here for it.

For now, revisit Alphonse Pierre’s review of the very non-Sabrina-esque Xavier.

entry.title: Jim James Announces Memoir One Wonders
entry.summary: “I hope the main thing someone takes away from this book (aside from learning more about the joys and challenges of being a working artist and musician) is that it’s okay to ask for help."
entry.content:
My Morning Jacket frontman Jim James has announced One Wonders, his first memoir, which will delve into the singer-songwriter’s upbringing in Louisville, the pitfalls of being a full-time musician, and his descent into and recovery from alcoholism and depression. It’s out April 13 on Simon & Schuster.

“If nothing else, I hope the main thing someone takes away from this book (aside from learning more about the joys and challenges of being a working artist and musician) is that it’s okay to ask for help,” James wrote in a heartfelt statement, which you can read in full below. “Everyone is going through some sort of challenge in this crazy world. IT IS POSSIBLE to find your way out of darkness and despair, and begin to enjoy the subtle, beautiful, everyday victories of simply being alive.”

In August, James premiered Wowed Out, his first solo album in eight years. He’ll be supporting it with a quick tour before the end of the year, kicking off with a hometown set in November; the full slate is listed below.

Jim James: One Wonders
$27.96 at Bookshop.org
$29 at Amazon

Hello, friends! I am releasing a memoir!

Why? Why write this book? Why now?

As I’ve made good progress in therapy over the last five or six years, I’ve been doing a lot of reflecting on finding my voice- both as a singer, songwriter and musician, and as a person wandering the earth wondering…

what do I really want to SAY with my life overall?

As I reflect on my own musical journey (from first learning to play the guitar to creating music in the present day) and navigating the complexities of life in general, I have been thinking a lot about my elders. For so many of them, tradition was to never speak about yourself. You carried your victories and failures, your joys and horrors, quietly.

A thought kept making its way into my mind: wouldn’t things be lighter for all of us if we shared more with other people?

I feel like it’s our generation’s job to tear down those walls and share our triumphs and horrors.

When we do, we’ll find that we’re all walking around with the same things inside of us, the good and the bad.

It helps so much when we can find a way to let them out together, so that we can all begin to move toward a more peaceful and love-centered existence.

As if it WANTED this to happen and was WILLING it to happen, the Universe stepped in and began to line up the things I needed to write this book, bring it to life, and ACTUALLY PUBLISH it. And I began to realize its purpose:

Perhaps if I illustrated my journey, and how I began to deal with my own struggles with mental health, it could help people take a step toward getting out of their own darkness and depression.

If nothing else, I hope the main thing someone takes away from this book (aside from learning more about the joys and challenges of being a working artist and musician) is that it’s okay to ask for help. Everyone is going through some sort of challenge in this crazy world. IT IS POSSIBLE to find your way out of darkness and despair, and begin to enjoy the subtle, beautiful, everyday victories of simply being alive.

One Wonders will be available April 13, 2027 in hardcover and ebook, and as an audiobook, which I'll be reading. Additionally, Carmichael's Bookstore in Louisville will have autographed copies that you can preorder now.
